newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM expects to survive challenge.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM expects to survive challenge.

text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, is expected to face down a parliamentary challenge on Wednesday by the secularist opposition.

Consensus calculations show the three main opposition factions, who agree on little but the desire to remove Erbakan as the head of secular, NATO-member Turkey, will come up short in a censure motion against the prime minister.

The opposition submitted three separate censure motions, later combined, in protest at the prime minister's visit to Libya, where he was lectured by leader Muammar Gaddafi for Turkey's treatment of its Kurdish minority.

On paper, the opposition needs 276 votes, a majority of the 550 seats, to guarantee victory. It can count on up to 269 MPs from its own ranks, plus a handful of dissidents from Erbakan's coalition ally the True Path Party.
The iron discipline of Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party all but bars defections.
A banner headline in the liberal Yeni Yuzyil summed up the likely outcome: "A censure motion in vain."
Erbakan, in office for little more than 100 days, radiated confidence ahead of parliament's debate and vote on the motion. If it does go through, a vote of confidance must be held within a week.

"This vote will strengthen the government further. The government will be a lot stronger, it will continue on its way," the veteran Welfare leader assured his parliamentary faction on Tuesday. "We will serve until the year 2000."
But looming economic, political and foreign policy worries suggest the sweet taste of victory will be short-lived.
Inflation is running at 80 percent, and many bankers and other analysts expect it to burst into triple digits.
Huge budget deficits have fed sky-high interest rates, robbing the economy of funds needed for investment. The Turkish lira, meanwhile, sinks against the dollar each passing day.
And foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have all warned of dire consequences if the government does not take matters in hand.

LIbya's snubbing of Erbakan and other perceived slights to Turkish honour at the hands of Gaddafi -- as well as Washington's public rebuke for the visit to a state it says sponsors terrorism -- offered the opposition a chance to displace the premier.
It also follows a series of other foreign policy gaffes and high-profile U-turns by Erbakan, heartening his critics and sparking vague grumblings among the secularist armed forces.
